law_name: Protocol Concerning the Redeployment in Hebron (Hebron Protocol)
description: Agreement signed with the Palestine Liberation Organization under Yasser Arafat in January 1997, under which Israel withdrew its troops from most of the West Bank city of Hebron. According to Britannica, it marked Netanyahu's reversal of his earlier opposition to the 1993 Oslo Accords.
significance: First agreement under the Oslo framework signed by a Likud government. Its cabinet approval was at the centre of the 1997 Bar-On affair investigation (see justice).

description: Agreement negotiated with Yasser Arafat at the Wye River talks hosted by US President Bill Clinton in October 1998, setting out steps to implement the 1995 Interim Agreement, including placing as much as 40% of the West Bank under Palestinian control according to Britannica. The Knesset approved it by 75 votes to 19 on 17 November 1998 (Wikipedia).
significance: Opposed by right-wing groups; several factions left Netanyahu's coalition, the Knesset voted for early elections and he lost the May 1999 election.

law_name: Basic Law: Israel as the Nation-State of the Jewish People (חוק יסוד: ישראל – מדינת הלאום של העם היהודי)
description: Basic Law passed on 19 July 2018 by 62 votes to 55 with two abstentions under Netanyahu's fourth government. It enshrines Israel as ‘the national home of the Jewish people’, declares Jerusalem the capital, sets the Hebrew calendar as the official calendar, recognises Jewish holidays and downgrades Arabic from an official language to one with a ‘special’ status, while stating that its prior status is not harmed. Netanyahu called it ‘a pivotal moment in the annals of Zionism and the State of Israel’.
significance: Critics, including Arab members of the Knesset, the EU and some US Jewish organisations, said it discriminates against Arab citizens and other minorities; proponents say it puts Jewish and democratic values on an equal footing.

law_name: Abraham Accords: normalisation agreements with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain (followed by Morocco and Sudan)
description: US-brokered agreements announced in a joint US–Israel–UAE statement on 13 August 2020 and signed in Washington in September 2020, establishing diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain; Morocco and Sudan followed. As part of the UAE deal, Israel agreed to ‘suspend declaring sovereignty’ over the West Bank areas set out in the Trump peace plan.
significance: Israel's first normalisation agreements with Arab states since the peace treaties with Egypt (1979) and Jordan (1994); they did not involve the Palestinians.

law_name: Amendment to Basic Law: The Government on declaring a prime minister incapacitated (‘recusal law’)
description: Amendment passed in March 2023 limiting the grounds and procedure for declaring a prime minister incapacitated to the government and the Knesset with special majorities, which, according to the Times of Israel, shields Netanyahu from being ordered to step aside by the attorney general or the High Court over his conflict of interest.
significance: On 3 January 2024 the High Court ruled 6–5 that the law was ‘clearly personal’ in purpose and postponed its application to the next Knesset, after the 2026 election.

law_name: Basic Law: The Judiciary, Amendment No. 3 (limitation of the reasonableness standard)
description: Passed in July 2023 as the only part of the original judicial overhaul package to become law, it barred all courts from reviewing government and ministerial decisions on the ground of extreme unreasonableness.
significance: Annulled by the High Court of Justice on 1 January 2024 by eight votes to seven, the first time the court struck down a Basic Law amendment; 13 of the 15 justices affirmed the court's authority to review Basic Laws.

law_name: Laws barring UNRWA from operating in Israel and banning state contact with the agency
description: Two laws passed on 28 October 2024, by 92–10 and 87–9, barring the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) from operating in Israeli territory, including East Jerusalem, and banning Israeli state authorities from contact with it, which severely limits its work in Gaza and the West Bank. Lawmakers cited the alleged involvement of UNRWA staff in terrorism.
significance: UNRWA said the laws breach the UN Charter and Israel's obligations under international law, and the UN Secretary-General and many governments criticised them; Netanyahu's office said Israel was ready to work with international partners to ensure aid reached Gaza.

law_name: Amendment to Basic Law: The Judiciary on the composition of the Judicial Selection Committee
description: Passed on 27 March 2025, the law changes the committee that appoints judges, giving coalition and opposition politicians control over nominations and exclusive power over Supreme Court appointments, with a mechanism allowing each side to choose justices after a year of deadlock. It takes effect only when the next Knesset is sworn in.
significance: Justice Minister Yariv Levin said it would diversify the bench; opposition parties and legal scholars said it would politicise the judiciary and vowed to repeal it. Petitions are pending; at a June 2026 hearing nine of the 11 justices strongly criticised it.

law_name: Death Penalty for Terrorists Law, 2026 (חוק עונש מוות למחבלים)
description: Passed on 30 March 2026 by 62 votes to 48, with Netanyahu voting in favour. According to the Times of Israel it makes death by hanging the default sentence for West Bank residents convicted by military courts of deadly terrorist acts, allowing life imprisonment only in vaguely defined ‘special circumstances’, by a simple majority of judges.
significance: A long-standing demand of Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit. Critics, including the Knesset committee's legal adviser and a UN body, call it discriminatory; petitions have been filed with the High Court. Israel has carried out the death penalty only twice, most recently against Adolf Eichmann in 1962.

law_name: Temporary law suspending the arrest and prosecution of ultra-Orthodox draft evaders
description: Passed on 14 July 2026 by 58 votes to 54 as part of an agreement between Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox parties, it grants yeshiva students evading military service immunity from arrest and prosecution until late January 2027 and suspends ongoing proceedings. IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir called it ‘inconceivable’ and inconsistent with the army's needs; some 72,000 Haredi men aged 18 to 24 were eligible for service but had not enlisted.
significance: The High Court of Justice froze the law pending a hearing; Deputy Foreign Minister Sharren Haskel resigned in protest.

law_name: Law restructuring the powers and appointment of the Attorney General
description: Passed on 15 July 2026 by 65 votes to 51 after an eleven-hour filibuster, it allows ministers to reject the attorney general's legal positions, which have been binding on the government since a 1993 High Court ruling, and gives the government effective control over appointing and dismissing the attorney general. Provisions on the attorney general's role as head of the prosecution were removed to speed its passage. It is due to take effect in January 2027.
significance: Politicians on both right and left have argued that the attorney general has too much power to restrict government action; opponents of the law say it removes one of the few checks on executive power. Petitions are pending before the High Court.

law_name: Communications (broadcasting and media regulation) overhaul law
description: Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi's law, passed on 16–17 July 2026 by 53 votes to 48, overhauls broadcast regulation, removing oversight mechanisms, minimum journalistic standards, local-production obligations and cross-ownership limits, and giving the government greater influence over ratings measurement and state advertising.
significance: Critics say it expands government control over the media; the Times of Israel noted that Karhi's statement that Netanyahu had tasked him with the reform appeared to conflict with Netanyahu's conflict-of-interest arrangement. Petitions citing procedural flaws are pending.

law_name: Extension of mandatory military service for men to 32 months
description: Passed just before the Knesset dispersed on 17 July 2026, by 43 votes to 12, it extends compulsory service for male soldiers from 30 to 32 months until June 2029, against the IDF's request for 36 months amid manpower shortages.
significance: The army said it urgently needed 12,000 additional recruits; the extension was passed in the same week as the law suspending the arrest of ultra-Orthodox draft evaders.
